strengths: Important and well-motivated problem formulation: Prior works on typographic robustness predominantly focus on object recognition by suppressing text reading, which degrades LVLM performance on genuine text-reading tasks. Formalizing 'selective text use' addresses a critical blind spot in multimodal robustness.

Rigorously designed same-scene counterfactual benchmark (RIO-Bench): By leveraging images with dual annotations (Open Images and TextVQA), the benchmark controls for visual scene confounders across four complementary conditions (Object/Text × Clean/Attacked).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: Experiments span multiple modern LVLM architectures and scales (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen-2.5-VL, Qwen-3-VL, LLaMA-3.2-Vision, SmolVLM), demonstrating the broad failure of existing models and defenses to achieve selective text use.

Insightful analysis of parameter placement and mechanisms: The ablation comparing vision encoder vs. language model fine-tuning reveals that selective text handling is primarily orchestrated by the LLM reasoning component rather than the vision encoder, challenging prevailing vision-centric defense paradigms in CLIP-era literature.

Thorough generalization and attention analysis: Out-of-domain evaluation on Typo-D and multiple text-centric VQA benchmarks (AI2D, ChartQA, DocVQA, InfoVQA), along with relative attention heatmaps, provides strong supporting evidence for the findings.
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty of the defense method: The proposed defense (RIO-RT) is essentially standard LoRA-based supervised fine-tuning on a balanced mixture of attacked object- and text-centric data. While effective in demonstrating the value of the benchmark's training split, it represents a straightforward data-augmentation/SFT baseline rather than an architectural or algorithmic innovation.

Synthetic nature and potential ambiguity of typographic attacks: The overlaid text attacks are rendered with synthetic fonts and bounding box heuristics. In the Text-Attack generation, prompting LLaMA-3 to generate contradictory words at mid/far distance could occasionally create unnatural scenes or ambiguous multi-text contexts where human baseline agreement might vary.

Minor presentation inconsistencies: In Section 5.1.1 the text lists Qwen3-VL-8B, whereas Table 1 refers to Qwen-3-VL-7B. Clarifying model checkpoints and reporting standard errors/variances over multiple random seeds would further solidify the results.

strengths: Compelling and timely problem formulation: The paper clearly identifies a critical flaw in current typographic attack literature—namely, that existing defenses achieve robustness by blindly suppressing text-reading ability. Formalizing the trade-off through 'selective text use' in Read-or-Ignore VQA (RIO-VQA) is conceptually sound and practically important.

Rigorously controlled benchmark design: Leveraging dual-annotated images from TextVQA and Open Images allows the construction of same-scene counterfactuals across a 2x2 grid (Object vs. Text questions, Clean vs. Attacked images). This holds the visual scene constant and directly isolates the read-vs-ignore behavior from confounding scene variations.

Principled attack generation: The use of the Open Images semantic hierarchy to craft easy/medium/hard object-level distractors, combined with LLM-generated contradictory distractors placed at calibrated spatial distances for text-level attacks, ensures systematic difficulty grading.

Comprehensive empirical analysis and insightful findings: The authors evaluate six diverse LVLM architectures and analyze parameter placement (LoRA on Vision vs. Language vs. V+L). The finding that selective text use is primarily driven by the language model's reasoning rather than the vision encoder provides valuable architectural insight contrary to earlier CLIP-era defenses.

Thorough generalization and qualitative validation: The supplementary material provides extensive evaluations on out-of-domain benchmarks (Typo-D and four text-centric VQA benchmarks), token-level attention visualizations, and training data size scaling curves.
weaknesses: Synthetic overlay methodology: Injected typographic attacks rely on basic 2D font rendering over bounding-box-free areas. While controlled, it lacks the physical realism, perspective distortion, and natural lighting integration found in generative or physical typographic attacks (e.g., SceneTAP).

Limited algorithmic novelty of the defense: RIO-RT is essentially standard multi-task supervised fine-tuning (LoRA SFT) on a balanced mixture of the benchmark's training split. While it effectively demonstrates that balanced training mitigates the trade-off, it represents an empirical proof-of-concept rather than a novel defense mechanism or architectural formulation.

Reliance on CLIP for Object-OE evaluation: The proposed Robust-CLIP-Match (R-CLIP-M) relies on CLIP text-text similarity. Given that CLIP encoders exhibit their own semantic biases and lack fine-grained sensitivity to negation/compositionality, this metric may introduce subtle evaluation biases.

strengths: Important and well-motivated problem formulation: Prior works on typographic robustness predominantly focus on object recognition, which unintentionally rewards models for ignoring text altogether and severely compromises their OCR and text-reading capabilities. Framing the problem as 'selective text use' (Read-or-Ignore) addresses a critical blind spot in LVLM evaluation.

Rigorous counterfactual benchmark design: By leveraging dual-annotated images from TextVQA and Open Images, RIO-Bench provides matched, same-scene counterfactuals across a 2x2 grid (Object vs. Text questions crossed with Clean vs. Attacked images). This holds the underlying visual context constant and cleanly isolates selective text use from scene-level confounds.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: The authors benchmark a wide suite of modern open-source LVLMs across different scales and families (LLaVA-1.5, Qwen-2.5-VL, Qwen-3-VL, Llama-3.2-Vision, SmolVLM-2B). The empirical results convincingly substantiate that existing defenses (e.g., CoT or text-suppression training) cause significant collateral damage to text reading.

Insightful architectural ablations and visualizations: The LoRA parameter placement ablation (Table 2) provides a compelling insight that selective text use is predominantly governed by the language component rather than the vision encoder, directly challenging prior vision-centric defense paradigms. The layer-wise attention visualizations in Figure 5 further elucidate how representations shift across layers.
weaknesses: Synthetic attack realism and visual simplicity: The typographic attacks are generated via synthetic 2D text overlays using a single font (DejaVuSans) rendered into unoccupied rectangular regions. Real-world typographic attacks often involve perspective distortions, surface textures, lighting/shadow variations, or physical stickers (as studied in SceneTAP or SCAM). It remains an open question whether models trained/evaluated on these clean digital text overlays transfer effectively to organically blended scene text.

Methodological novelty of the proposed defense (RIO-RT): While RIO-Bench is the primary contribution, the proposed defense RIO-RT is essentially standard multi-task supervised fine-tuning (LoRA SFT) on a balanced mixture of attack variations. While it serves as a solid baseline showing that data-driven balanced exposure helps, the defense itself does not introduce novel architectural or algorithmic mechanisms.

Risk of distribution over-fitting between train and test splits: RIO-RT is trained on a subset of the RIO-Bench training distribution, which shares similar font styling, rendering properties, and distractor generation prompts (via LLaMA-3) with the evaluation set. Although Table 4 tests out-of-domain transfer to Typo-D and standard text-VQA datasets, evaluation against diverse unseen attack fonts, cursive scripts, or adversarially optimized typographic placements is limited.

Ground truth selection heuristics for Object-VQA: The selection of the single ground-truth object class via CLIP image-text similarity among Open Images labels could potentially introduce noisy or biased labels, especially in complex multi-object scenes.

strengths: Important and well-motivated problem formulation: The paper identifies a critical blind spot in current typographic attack research, namely that existing defenses often achieve apparent robustness in object recognition simply by suppressing textual sensitivity ('ignoring text'), which severely degrades the model's scene-text reading capabilities.

Principled counterfactual benchmark design: By leveraging images with dual annotations from TextVQA and Open Images, RIO-Bench holds the underlying visual scene constant while systematically crossing question intent (object vs. text) and attack condition (clean vs. attack), effectively isolating read-or-ignore behavior while minimizing scene-level confounding factors.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation and analysis: The benchmark tests a wide variety of LVLM architectures and scales (from 2B up to 38B, as well as frontier models), incorporating both synthetic digital overlays and scene-coherent generative insertions (SceneTAP). The ablations (LoRA placement across vision vs. language backbones) and attention visualizations offer valuable diagnostic insights.

High quality validation and out-of-domain transfer: Benchmark quality is validated with a rigorous human audit exhibiting high inter-annotator agreement (Gwet's AC1 ~0.89–0.94), and generalization experiments on Typo-D, AI2D, ChartQA, and DocVQA confirm the broader relevance of the findings.
weaknesses: Heuristic and simple baseline defense: RIO-RT is primarily a standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) recipe on a balanced mixture of attacked object- and text-centric samples. While it serves well as an empirical proof of concept, the paper does not propose a novel architectural mechanism or algorithmic formulation for dynamic context-dependent text filtering.

Potential artifacts from automated distractor generation: Distractor words and open-ended text attack targets are generated using LLM prompts (Llama-3) and class hierarchies, which may introduce semantic biases or distribution shifts relative to purely natural or adversarial typographic attacks.

Limited coverage of real-world physical attacks: While SceneTAP provides generative insertions, the evaluated threat models are still predominantly planar digital overlays and localized inpaintings, lacking complex physical-world variations such as perspective distortions, curved surfaces (e.g., clothing folds, bottles), or non-uniform illumination/shadowing.

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated problem: The paper identifies a significant blind spot in current typographic attack evaluations, namely that existing defenses often achieve robustness by indiscriminately suppressing text sensitivity, severely impairing the model's essential ability to read genuine scene text.

Sound counterfactual benchmark design: By pairing object annotations and scene-text QA on the same underlying images from TextVQA/Open Images, RIO-Bench isolates read-or-ignore behavior across four complementary conditions (Obj/Text x Clean/Attack) while controlling for background visual confounds.

Rigorous attack construction and quality control: Hierarchical negative sampling from the Open Images taxonomy provides principled difficulty tiers for object distractors, text placement avoids genuine text occlusions, and human audit with inter-rater reliability metrics confirms dataset quality.

Comprehensive empirical investigation and insightful analysis: The benchmark evaluates multiple LVLM families across scales, including attention map visualizations and LoRA parameter localization ablations, demonstrating that selective read-or-ignore behavior is largely driven by language-model reasoning rather than vision encoder adaptation.

Thorough transfer and generalization experiments: Evaluating generalization to both an external typographic attack benchmark (Typo-D) and multiple text-centric VQA benchmarks (AI2D, ChartQA, DocVQA, InfoVQA) convincingly substantiates the trade-off and baseline behavior.
weaknesses: Baseline defense relies primarily on standard SFT: While RIO-RT is explicitly presented as a minimal reference baseline, it relies on direct fine-tuning on a balanced mixture of attacked pairs rather than proposing a novel architecture, loss formulation, or inference-time mechanism.

Reliance on synthetic distractors: Although SceneTAP provides scene-coherent generative insertions to complement digital overlays, both insertion schemes remain synthetically injected perturbations rather than naturally occurring ambiguous physical signage.
Model nomenclature clarity: Table 5 includes references to closed-source frontier models (e.g., 'GPT-5.4'), which appears non-standard or hypothetical and should be properly clarified or verified.

strengths: Compelling and practically relevant conceptual framing: The paper identifies a critical flaw in existing typographic robustness literature, namely that prevailing defenses can achieve robustness in object-centric tasks merely by suppressing text sensitivity ('ignoring all text'), which severely compromises essential scene-text reading capabilities. Formulating the 'Read-or-Ignore' paradigm within the same visual scene directly addresses this misalignment.

Rigorous same-scene counterfactual benchmark design: By pairing TextVQA annotations with Open Images object hierarchy labels on identical images, RIO-Bench controls for background and visual confounders across four distinct quadrants (Obj/Text × Clean/Attack). The inclusion of multiple difficulty levels (semantic proximity for objects, spatial proximity for text) and realistic generative insertions (SceneTAP) adds solid diagnostic depth.

Thorough quality validation and metric design: The introduction of R-CLIP-M appropriately addresses the limitation of standard retrieval metrics under distractor attacks. Additionally, the human audit across 400 samples with strong inter-rater reliability (Gwet's AC1 between 0.89–0.94) provides confidence in benchmark annotation quality.

Extensive empirical evaluation and insightful analyses: The manuscript evaluates a comprehensive suite of models ranging from small/medium open-source models (LLaVA-1.5, SmolVLM, Qwen2.5/3-VL, InternVL-3.5, Llama-3.2-Vision) to closed-source frontier models (GPT-5.4, Gemini-2.5-Pro). The ablation demonstrating that language model tuning (rather than vision encoder tuning alone) drives selective read-or-ignore resolution, along with attention map visualizations and out-of-distribution transfer (Typo-D, DocVQA, ChartQA, AI2D), provides valuable mechanistic and practical takeaways.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty on the defense side: While the paper frames RIO-RT as a minimal reference baseline, it relies solely on standard supervised fine-tuning / LoRA on a balanced mixture of attacked pairs. Exploring more principled architectural mechanisms, routing strategies, or training objectives specifically tailored to distinguish genuine scene text from adversarial distractors would make the technical contribution much stronger.

Templated nature of the Object-Centric VQA questions: The newly generated object-centric questions (both multiple-choice and open-ended) rely on uniform synthetic templates ('Which object is present in the image?', 'What objects can be seen in the image?'). This linguistic simplicity contrasts with the natural linguistic diversity of TextVQA questions and may introduce stylistic shortcuts for models during evaluation and fine-tuning.

Scope of threat model and distractor realism: Although SceneTAP is evaluated, the majority of the benchmark and all fine-tuning rely on axis-aligned digital overlays with synthetic font rendering. Physical typographic attacks (e.g., printed stickers on curved 3D surfaces, viewpoint variations, illumination changes) and adversarially optimized token texts remain unexplored.
